title: Electronics I
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 200L introductory analog electronics curriculum: semiconductor physics, p-n junction diodes and their applications (rectification, Zener regulation, LEDs), bipolar junction transistors and basic amplification, plus basic passive RC/RL circuit behaviour and a brief intro to logic gates. Advanced digital electronics, op-amps, and oscillators are reserved for PHY307 (Electronics II).

questions.question: An intrinsic semiconductor is best described as:
options: A pure semiconductor material with no significant impurities added
A semiconductor that has been deliberately doped with impurity atoms
A material that conducts electricity as well as a metal at room temperature
A perfect insulator with zero free charge carriers at any temperature
questions.correct_answer: A pure semiconductor material with no significant impurities added
questions.explanation: Intrinsic semiconductors, such as pure silicon or germanium, contain no significant impurity doping, and their conductivity arises solely from thermally generated electron-hole pairs.

questions.question: In an intrinsic semiconductor at a given temperature, the number of free electrons compared to the number of holes is:
options: Equal
Always greater than the number of holes
Always less than the number of holes
Exactly zero for both
questions.correct_answer: Equal
questions.explanation: In a pure (intrinsic) semiconductor, every thermally excited electron that jumps to the conduction band leaves behind a hole in the valence band, so electron and hole concentrations are equal.

questions.question: An extrinsic semiconductor is produced by:
options: Deliberately adding a small, controlled amount of impurity atoms (doping) to a pure semiconductor
Heating a pure semiconductor to extremely high temperatures
Removing all impurities from a semiconductor crystal
Cooling a semiconductor to near absolute zero
questions.correct_answer: Deliberately adding a small, controlled amount of impurity atoms (doping) to a pure semiconductor
questions.explanation: Doping introduces controlled impurities into an intrinsic semiconductor to significantly alter and control its electrical conductivity, producing an extrinsic semiconductor.

questions.question: An n-type semiconductor is formed by doping a pure semiconductor (e.g. silicon) with:
options: A pentavalent (Group V) impurity such as phosphorus or arsenic, which donates extra free electrons
A trivalent (Group III) impurity such as boron, which creates extra holes
Another sample of pure silicon with no valence difference
A noble gas element with a full valence shell
questions.correct_answer: A pentavalent (Group V) impurity such as phosphorus or arsenic, which donates extra free electrons
questions.explanation: Pentavalent impurities have five valence electrons; four form covalent bonds with silicon, leaving one extra electron that becomes a free charge carrier, hence 'n-type' (negative charge carriers).

questions.question: A p-type semiconductor is formed by doping a pure semiconductor with:
options: A trivalent (Group III) impurity such as boron or gallium, which creates extra holes
A pentavalent (Group V) impurity such as phosphorus
A tetravalent (Group IV) impurity identical to the host material
A metal with very high conductivity
questions.correct_answer: A trivalent (Group III) impurity such as boron or gallium, which creates extra holes
questions.explanation: Trivalent impurities have only three valence electrons, leaving one covalent bond incomplete, which creates a 'hole' that acts as a positive charge carrier, hence 'p-type'.

questions.question: In an n-type semiconductor, the majority charge carriers are:
options: Free electrons
Holes
Protons
Neutral atoms
questions.correct_answer: Free electrons
questions.explanation: In n-type material, the donor impurities contribute a surplus of free electrons, making electrons the majority carriers, while holes (from thermal generation) are the minority carriers.

questions.question: In a p-type semiconductor, the minority charge carriers are:
options: Electrons
Holes
Protons
Ions
questions.correct_answer: Electrons
questions.explanation: In p-type material, holes (contributed by acceptor impurities) are the majority carriers, while thermally generated electrons are present in much smaller numbers as minority carriers.

questions.question: A p-n junction diode is formed by:
options: Joining a p-type semiconductor region and an n-type semiconductor region within a single crystal
Joining two identical p-type semiconductor regions
Connecting a metal directly to an insulator
Joining two identical n-type semiconductor regions
questions.correct_answer: Joining a p-type semiconductor region and an n-type semiconductor region within a single crystal
questions.explanation: A p-n junction is created at the interface between p-type and n-type regions of the same semiconductor crystal, forming the basic building block of the diode.

questions.question: The depletion region (depletion layer) at a p-n junction is formed by:
options: Diffusion of majority carriers across the junction, leaving behind fixed immobile ions and a region depleted of free charge carriers
The complete removal of all dopant atoms near the junction
An externally applied magnetic field
Cooling the junction to very low temperatures
questions.correct_answer: Diffusion of majority carriers across the junction, leaving behind fixed immobile ions and a region depleted of free charge carriers
questions.explanation: Near the junction, electrons diffuse from the n-side and holes diffuse from the p-side, recombining and leaving behind fixed charged ions, creating a narrow region depleted of mobile carriers and an internal electric field (barrier potential).

questions.question: The typical barrier (built-in) potential of a silicon p-n junction diode at room temperature is approximately:
questions.explanation: Silicon diodes typically have a barrier potential of about 0.6-0.7 V, compared to about 0.3 V for germanium diodes.

questions.question: When a p-n junction diode is forward biased:
options: The p-type region is connected to the positive terminal and the n-type region to the negative terminal, narrowing the depletion region and allowing current to flow easily
The p-type region is connected to the negative terminal and the n-type region to the positive terminal, widening the depletion region
No current flows under any circumstances
The diode behaves exactly like an open circuit at all voltages
questions.correct_answer: The p-type region is connected to the positive terminal and the n-type region to the negative terminal, narrowing the depletion region and allowing current to flow easily
questions.explanation: Forward biasing reduces the depletion region width and barrier potential, allowing majority carriers to flow across the junction once the applied voltage exceeds the threshold (cut-in) voltage.

questions.question: When a p-n junction diode is reverse biased:
options: The depletion region widens and only a very small leakage (reverse saturation) current flows
The depletion region narrows and current flows freely
The diode conducts exactly as well as in forward bias
The diode is destroyed instantly regardless of the reverse voltage magnitude
questions.correct_answer: The depletion region widens and only a very small leakage (reverse saturation) current flows
questions.explanation: In reverse bias, the applied voltage widens the depletion region and increases the barrier, allowing only a small reverse saturation current due to minority carriers, until breakdown occurs at sufficiently high reverse voltage.

questions.question: The current-voltage (I-V) characteristic curve of a p-n junction diode shows that:
options: Current increases sharply (exponentially) once the forward voltage exceeds a threshold, while reverse current remains very small until breakdown
Current increases linearly with voltage in both forward and reverse bias, like a resistor
Current is completely independent of applied voltage
Reverse current is always larger than forward current
questions.correct_answer: Current increases sharply (exponentially) once the forward voltage exceeds a threshold, while reverse current remains very small until breakdown
questions.explanation: The diode's I-V characteristic is highly non-linear: negligible current flows below the forward threshold voltage, then current rises steeply (approximately exponentially), while reverse bias produces only a tiny leakage current until avalanche or Zener breakdown.

questions.question: The cut-in (threshold/knee) voltage of a diode is:
options: The forward voltage at which the diode begins to conduct significantly
The maximum reverse voltage the diode can withstand
The voltage at which the diode always fails permanently
A voltage that applies only in reverse bias
questions.correct_answer: The forward voltage at which the diode begins to conduct significantly
questions.explanation: Below the cut-in voltage, forward current is negligible; once the applied forward voltage exceeds this threshold (about 0.7 V for silicon), current rises rapidly.

questions.question: A half-wave rectifier circuit uses a single diode to:
options: Allow current to flow during only one half-cycle of the AC input, blocking the other half
Allow current to flow during both half-cycles of the AC input
Convert DC voltage into AC voltage
Amplify the AC input signal
questions.correct_answer: Allow current to flow during only one half-cycle of the AC input, blocking the other half
questions.explanation: A half-wave rectifier conducts only when the diode is forward biased (one half-cycle of the AC waveform), producing a pulsating output for that half only and blocking the other half.

questions.question: A full-wave rectifier, compared to a half-wave rectifier, produces an output that:
options: Utilizes both halves of the AC input cycle, giving a higher average output voltage and smoother pulsating DC
Utilizes only one half of the AC cycle, exactly like a half-wave rectifier
Produces pure, ripple-free DC without any filtering needed
Cannot be achieved using diodes at all
questions.correct_answer: Utilizes both halves of the AC input cycle, giving a higher average output voltage and smoother pulsating DC
questions.explanation: Full-wave rectification converts both halves of the AC input into output pulses of the same polarity, resulting in a higher average DC output and less ripple than half-wave rectification.

questions.question: A bridge rectifier circuit uses how many diodes to achieve full-wave rectification?
options: Four
Two
One
Six
questions.correct_answer: Four
questions.explanation: A bridge rectifier arranges four diodes so that current always flows through the load in the same direction for both halves of the AC cycle, without requiring a centre-tapped transformer.

questions.question: One advantage of a bridge rectifier over a centre-tapped full-wave rectifier is that:
options: It does not require a centre-tapped transformer
It uses fewer diodes
It only rectifies one half of the AC cycle
It cannot handle high currents
questions.correct_answer: It does not require a centre-tapped transformer
questions.explanation: The bridge rectifier achieves full-wave rectification using an ordinary transformer (or no transformer at all), unlike the centre-tapped rectifier which needs a special transformer with a centre tap, though it uses more diodes.

questions.question: A Zener diode is specifically designed to operate in which region of its characteristic curve?
options: The reverse breakdown region
The forward conduction region only
The cut-off region only
It has no distinct operating region
questions.correct_answer: The reverse breakdown region
questions.explanation: Unlike ordinary diodes, Zener diodes are designed to operate safely in reverse breakdown, where the voltage across them remains nearly constant over a range of currents.

questions.question: A Zener diode is commonly used as a voltage regulator because:
options: It maintains a nearly constant voltage across itself once it enters reverse breakdown, despite variations in current
It amplifies voltage signals like a transistor
It converts AC to DC more efficiently than a bridge rectifier
It blocks all current in both forward and reverse bias
questions.correct_answer: It maintains a nearly constant voltage across itself once it enters reverse breakdown, despite variations in current
questions.explanation: Once operating in the breakdown (Zener) region, the voltage across the diode stays essentially constant over a wide current range, making it ideal for stabilizing (regulating) a voltage supply.

questions.question: A light-emitting diode (LED) emits light when:
options: It is forward biased and electrons recombine with holes at the junction, releasing energy as photons
It is reverse biased beyond its breakdown voltage
No current flows through it at all
It is cooled to a very low temperature
questions.correct_answer: It is forward biased and electrons recombine with holes at the junction, releasing energy as photons
questions.explanation: In a forward-biased LED, electron-hole recombination at the junction releases energy directly as photons of light (rather than heat, as in ordinary diodes), a phenomenon called electroluminescence.

questions.question: The colour (wavelength) of light emitted by an LED is primarily determined by:
options: The band gap energy of the semiconductor material used
The physical size of the LED casing
The ambient room temperature only
The polarity of the power supply
questions.correct_answer: The band gap energy of the semiconductor material used
questions.explanation: The energy (and hence wavelength/colour) of photons emitted during recombination is determined by the semiconductor's band gap; different compound semiconductors (e.g. GaAs, GaP, GaN) are used to produce different LED colours.

questions.question: A bipolar junction transistor (BJT) has how many terminals?
options: Three: emitter, base, and collector
Two: anode and cathode
Four: source, gate, drain, and body
Five terminals
questions.correct_answer: Three: emitter, base, and collector
questions.explanation: A BJT is a three-terminal semiconductor device with an emitter, a base, and a collector, formed by two back-to-back p-n junctions.

questions.question: An NPN transistor consists of:
options: A thin p-type base region sandwiched between two n-type regions (emitter and collector)
A thin n-type base region sandwiched between two p-type regions
Three n-type regions joined together with no p-type material
A single p-type region only
questions.correct_answer: A thin p-type base region sandwiched between two n-type regions (emitter and collector)
questions.explanation: In an NPN transistor, the structure is n-type emitter, p-type base, and n-type collector; the reverse (PNP) has a thin n-type base between two p-type regions.

questions.question: For normal (active-mode) transistor operation as an amplifier, the emitter-base junction and collector-base junction should be biased as follows:
options: Emitter-base junction forward biased, collector-base junction reverse biased
Both junctions forward biased
Both junctions reverse biased
Emitter-base junction reverse biased, collector-base junction forward biased
questions.correct_answer: Emitter-base junction forward biased, collector-base junction reverse biased
questions.explanation: In active mode (used for amplification), the emitter-base junction is forward biased to inject carriers into the base, while the collector-base junction is reverse biased to collect them, producing current gain.

questions.question: In a BJT, the base region is deliberately made:
options: Very thin and lightly doped
Very thick and heavily doped
The same thickness as the emitter and collector
Made of a different element entirely from the rest of the transistor
questions.correct_answer: Very thin and lightly doped
questions.explanation: A thin, lightly doped base allows most carriers injected from the emitter to pass through to the collector rather than recombining in the base, which is essential for good current gain.

questions.question: The DC current gain (β or h_FE) of a BJT is defined as the ratio of:
options: Collector current to base current (I_C/I_B)
Base current to collector current (I_B/I_C)
Emitter current to base current (I_E/I_B) only, never involving collector current
Collector current to emitter current squared
questions.correct_answer: Collector current to base current (I_C/I_B)
questions.explanation: Current gain β = I_C/I_B describes how much the small base current is amplified to produce a much larger collector current, typically ranging from tens to a few hundred for common transistors.

questions.question: In a BJT, the relationship between emitter current (I_E), base current (I_B), and collector current (I_C) is:
options: I_E = I_B + I_C
I_E = I_B − I_C
I_E = I_B × I_C
I_C = I_E + I_B
questions.correct_answer: I_E = I_B + I_C
questions.explanation: By Kirchhoff's current law applied to the transistor, the emitter current equals the sum of the base and collector currents.

questions.question: A transistor has a base current of 50 μA and a current gain β of 100. What is the collector current?
options: 5 mA
0.5 mA
50 mA
150 μA
questions.correct_answer: 5 mA

questions.question: In a basic common-emitter (CE) amplifier configuration, the emitter terminal is:
options: Common to both the input and output circuits
Used only for the output signal, never the input
Left completely disconnected
Connected directly to the collector at all times
questions.correct_answer: Common to both the input and output circuits
questions.explanation: In the common-emitter configuration, the input signal is applied between base and emitter, and the output is taken between collector and emitter, making the emitter the shared (common) terminal.

questions.question: A key characteristic of the common-emitter amplifier configuration is that it provides:
options: Both current gain and voltage gain, with a 180° phase inversion between input and output
Voltage gain only, with no current gain and no phase inversion
Neither current gain nor voltage gain
Current gain only, with the output in phase with the input
questions.correct_answer: Both current gain and voltage gain, with a 180° phase inversion between input and output
questions.explanation: The common-emitter amplifier is widely used because it provides significant current and voltage amplification, though the output signal is inverted (180° out of phase) relative to the input.

questions.question: The purpose of biasing a transistor amplifier circuit with resistors and a DC supply is to:
options: Establish a stable operating (quiescent) point so the transistor amplifies the AC signal without distortion
Convert the transistor into a pure switch with no amplification
Eliminate the need for a power supply entirely
Ensure the transistor conducts only during reverse bias
questions.correct_answer: Establish a stable operating (quiescent) point so the transistor amplifies the AC signal without distortion
questions.explanation: Proper DC biasing sets the transistor's quiescent (Q) point in the active region so that the applied AC signal can swing without driving the transistor into cut-off or saturation, avoiding distortion.

questions.question: In a simple RC low-pass filter circuit (resistor and capacitor in series, output taken across the capacitor), the circuit tends to:
options: Pass low-frequency signals while attenuating high-frequency signals
Pass high-frequency signals while attenuating low-frequency signals
Attenuate all frequencies equally regardless of value
Amplify all frequencies above a certain threshold
questions.correct_answer: Pass low-frequency signals while attenuating high-frequency signals
questions.explanation: At low frequencies, the capacitor's reactance is high, so most of the input voltage appears across it (output); at high frequencies, the capacitor's reactance drops, shorting out the output, hence a low-pass response.

questions.question: In an RC high-pass filter (output taken across the resistor), which frequencies are passed with little attenuation?
options: High-frequency signals
Low-frequency signals
Only DC (zero-frequency) signals
No signals are passed at any frequency
questions.correct_answer: High-frequency signals
questions.explanation: With the output taken across the resistor, high-frequency signals see low capacitor reactance and are passed through readily, while low-frequency (and DC) signals are blocked by the capacitor's high reactance.

questions.question: The cutoff frequency of an RC filter is given by:
options: f_c = 1/(2πRC)
f_c = 2πRC
f_c = RC
f_c = 1/(RC²)
questions.correct_answer: f_c = 1/(2πRC)
questions.explanation: The cutoff (or corner/half-power) frequency of a simple RC filter is defined by f_c = 1/(2πRC), where R is resistance in ohms and C is capacitance in farads.

questions.question: A capacitor in a DC circuit, once fully charged, behaves like:
options: An open circuit, blocking further DC current flow
A short circuit, allowing unlimited current
A resistor with fixed resistance equal to its capacitance value
An inductor
questions.correct_answer: An open circuit, blocking further DC current flow
questions.explanation: Once a capacitor is fully charged in a DC circuit, no further current flows through it, so it behaves like an open circuit under steady-state DC conditions.

questions.question: An inductor in a DC circuit, once current has reached steady state, behaves like:
options: A short circuit (ideally zero resistance)
An open circuit, blocking all current
A capacitor
A device with infinite resistance
questions.correct_answer: A short circuit (ideally zero resistance)
questions.explanation: In steady-state DC conditions, an ideal inductor offers no opposition to constant current flow (its induced EMF depends on the rate of change of current, which is zero at steady state), so it behaves like a short circuit.

questions.question: When an AC voltage is applied to a capacitor, its opposition to current flow (capacitive reactance, X_C) is given by:
options: X_C = 1/(2πfC)
X_C = 2πfC
X_C = 2πfL
X_C = f/C
questions.correct_answer: X_C = 1/(2πfC)
questions.explanation: Capacitive reactance decreases as frequency f or capacitance C increases, following X_C = 1/(2πfC), measured in ohms.

questions.question: A basic logic AND gate produces a HIGH (1) output only when:
options: All of its inputs are HIGH (1)
At least one input is HIGH (1)
All of its inputs are LOW (0)
Exactly one input is HIGH and the rest are LOW
questions.correct_answer: All of its inputs are HIGH (1)
questions.explanation: An AND gate outputs HIGH only when every one of its inputs is HIGH; if any input is LOW, the output is LOW, matching the truth table of logical conjunction.

questions.question: A basic logic OR gate produces a HIGH (1) output when:
options: At least one of its inputs is HIGH (1)
All of its inputs are HIGH (1) simultaneously only
All inputs are LOW (0)
Never, regardless of input
questions.correct_answer: At least one of its inputs is HIGH (1)
questions.explanation: An OR gate outputs HIGH if one or more of its inputs are HIGH, and outputs LOW only when all inputs are LOW.

questions.question: A NOT gate (inverter) is a logic gate that:
options: Produces an output that is the logical complement (opposite) of its single input
Requires at least two inputs to function
Always outputs HIGH regardless of input
Produces the same output as its input
questions.correct_answer: Produces an output that is the logical complement (opposite) of its single input
questions.explanation: A NOT gate is a single-input gate that inverts its input: a HIGH input produces a LOW output and vice versa.

questions.question: For a two-input AND gate with inputs A = 1 and B = 0, what is the output?
options: Undefined
Depends on a third input
questions.explanation: An AND gate requires both inputs HIGH to output HIGH; since B = 0, the output is 0 according to the AND truth table.

questions.question: Which of the following best distinguishes majority carriers from minority carriers in a doped semiconductor?
options: Majority carriers are the charge carrier type present in much greater number due to doping, while minority carriers are present in much smaller numbers, mainly from thermal generation
Majority carriers only exist at very high temperatures
Minority carriers move faster than majority carriers in all cases
Majority and minority carriers always exist in exactly equal numbers
questions.correct_answer: Majority carriers are the charge carrier type present in much greater number due to doping, while minority carriers are present in much smaller numbers, mainly from thermal generation
questions.explanation: Doping determines which carrier type dominates (majority) in a given semiconductor; the opposite carrier type remains present only in small numbers due to thermal generation (minority carriers).

questions.question: A filter capacitor is commonly added after a rectifier circuit in a power supply in order to:
options: Smooth out the pulsating DC output by reducing ripple
Convert the rectified DC back into pure AC
Increase the ripple in the output voltage
Block DC current entirely from reaching the load
questions.correct_answer: Smooth out the pulsating DC output by reducing ripple
questions.explanation: A filter (smoothing) capacitor charges during peaks of the rectified waveform and discharges slowly through the load during the troughs, reducing the ripple and producing a smoother, more constant DC output.
